summary: 40a resolves the right vs left hand lot dispute (right preferred, both valid); addresses the requirement for verbal designation ('chattat l'HaShem'); describes the crimson thread placement (half on Azazel goat, half on cliff) and the communication system (originally fire signals, later messengers after Samaritan interference).

display.whats: The right vs left hand lot dispute resolved; R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate.
display.hint: The lot is valid from either hand; if right draws 'for God' it is a good omen; the Deputy helps if needed.
display.title: Resolving the Right-Hand Lot Dispute

learning.ahaMoment: The lot ceremony's spiritual significance transcends technical hand requirements: God's acceptance is shown by the omen (right hand), not determined by it.
learning.memoryAnchor: Right hand = omen; left hand = still valid. The miracle was in the omen, not in invalidating the left.
learning.learnerQuestion: How does the Gemara resolve R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish's dispute over whether the right-hand lot is required?
learning.coreTension: R. Yochanan holds both hands are equally valid; Reish Lakish holds the right hand is required, two opposing positions on the same designation ceremony that the Gemara must reconcile into a working rule.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara resolves the dispute as preferred-but-not-required: the right hand is le-chatchila (the ideal way to perform it), while the left hand remains valid b'dieved (after the fact), with the Deputy assisting if the lot needs transferring.

takeaway.text: The right-hand 'for God' lot is the preferred, ideal outcome (le-chatchila), but a left-hand draw remains valid after the fact (b'dieved), the dispute resolves into a single graded rule rather than an either/or contradiction.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may read the resolution as simply 'right hand wins' or 'both are equal,' missing the le-chatchila/b'dieved distinction that actually reconciles the two positions.

misconceptions.misconception: The right-hand lot is absolutely required for the ceremony's validity; a left-hand draw invalidates the entire Yom Kippur designation.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara's resolution is graded, not absolute: the right hand is the ideal (le-chatchila) outcome, but a left-hand draw is valid after the fact (b'dieved). The dispute between R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish is resolved by distinguishing the preferred method from the minimum requirement for validity, not by ruling one position simply wrong.

quizSeeds.question: What is the halachic status of the 'for God' lot landing in the left hand?
quizSeeds.answer: It is valid post-facto; the right hand is preferred as a good omen but not strictly required.

sugyot.finalRuling: Right-hand lot is preferred (omen) but not required; verbal designation required; crimson thread split between goat and cliff.

rashiTranslations.en: Rather, according to that version you stated - they disagree in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yannai said
it is indispensable, and all the more so for Rabbi Nechemia - whose view is this? Neither Rabbi Yehuda's nor Rabbi
Nechemia's. It was taught: it is a mitzvah to place it - and if he did not place it, it is valid; and on this everyone
agrees, since regarding the placing the verse states it only one time, as it is written, 'and Aaron shall place,'
etc.; but regarding the rising, the verse states it,
as it is written, 'and Aaron shall offer the goat
upon which it came up,' etc., and it is written, 'and the goat
upon which it came up.' And to confess -
over the goat sent away, as it is written, 'and he shall confess over it,' etc.
If you say he did not place it - it is regarding that alone that
Rabbi Shimon says it is valid, but its rising from within
the urn, Rabbi Shimon holds, is indispensable.
But it was taught: if one of them dies - after the lottery,
since it is no longer possible to cast lots again unless
he brings two more and one goes to waste,
as stated in the chapter 'The Two Goats' (62a, below);
he brings one from the market in place of the one that died,
and it becomes the partner of the one still standing, and there is no
need to cast lots again. Rabbi Shimon did not know
etc. - it truly means that 'he did not cast lots,' which the first Tanna
says is valid, refers to 'he did not place it,' and your difficulty -
how can Rabbi Shimon say about that 'he did not cast lots, valid,'
if this casting of lots means the placing, implying that if
he did not lift it up it is invalid according to Rabbi Shimon - is not
a difficulty, since 'he did not cast lots,' as Rabbi Shimon
says, means literally 'he did not cast lots,' and he did not know
that 'he did not cast lots,' as the first Tanna says, refers to
the placing; and this is what Rabbi Shimon
says to the Rabbis: if you mean that 'he did not cast lots, valid,'
refers to the rising, which is the actual casting of lots,
I disagree with you in one point, absent the confession.
And if the casting of lots you mean is the placing -
but the rising, according to you, is indispensable, then I disagree
with you in two points, since for me the casting of lots is not indispensable
at all, while the confession is indispensable; and below it explains
the reason for both, in the confession. The bull is indispensable
to the goat - if he advanced one of the goat's
later services and performed it before the bull, the bull, which
is fitting to precede it, is indispensable and disqualifies it, and it does not
count for him, and he must go back and perform it after
the bull. And the order of their services is as follows,
as laid out in the passage: first he confesses over the bull,
the first confession, and then he casts lots on
the goat, and then he confesses over the bull again, the second confession, and slaughters it, and brings in the ladle
and the fire-pan, and places the incense on the coals, etc., and places some of the bull's blood on
the ark-cover; and then he slaughters the goat and places some of it on the ark-cover; and then
he places some of the bull's blood on the curtain, and then some of the goat's, and then
he mixes the bloods and places some on the inner altar. But the goat does not indispensably precede
the bull - if he advanced the bull's service, which is one of the later services relative to the goat,
and performed it before the goat, the goat, which was fitting to precede it, does not disqualify it.
Regarding the sprinklings that are done inside - they mean that the order of the bull is indispensable to the goat. If he advanced it
to the goat - regarding what is between the poles, before the bull, he has done nothing. But the goat does not
indispensably precede the bull, what is this - which service do we find performed for the goat
before the bull's inside sprinklings, that we should say about it that if he changed and advanced the bull's service before it,
the goat, which was fitting to precede it, does not disqualify it. In the Sanctuary - on the curtain. A statute
is written regarding them - for even Rabbi Yehuda concedes that regarding matters performed inside,
a statute is written, and here he changed the order in an inside service, since he advanced
the outside one, which is later than it, before it. Rather, is it not that he advanced the bull's sprinklings inside, before
the goat's lottery - since you can find no other goat-service that precedes the bull's

inside sprinklings except this one, and it teaches that it is not indispensable. And since the order is not indispensable, the lottery too is not indispensable - even if he uprooted it entirely; this implies there is someone

who says the lottery is not indispensable, and this is difficult for the one who says it is indispensable even according to Rabbi Yehuda, all the more so for Rabbi Nechemia - whose view is this? That he advanced the bull's sprinklings

on the inner altar, as it is written (Leviticus 16), 'and he shall take some of the bull's blood and some of the goat's blood,' etc., when he should have delayed it until the completion of the curtain sprinklings. And granted the order is not
indispensable, the lottery - since for Rabbi Yehuda a statute is not written regarding matters done outside - the lottery itself, when uprooted entirely, is indispensable, since the verse states
it explicitly, as we said. And they follow their own reasoning - this stands on the dispute over one who did not confess, and we read it before 'come and hear: the bull is indispensable to the goat.'
He shall stand - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (explaining that this teaches the requirement to bring a replacement goat if the first dies) continues on 40b.
